AREX – Airport Railroad
From Incheon Airport, the AREX Express runs non-stop to Seoul Station in about 45–50 min (about ₩11,000). The All-Stop train is cheaper (about ₩4,000–5,000), takes ~60 min and accepts T-money.
Airport limousine buses go directly to big hotel areas like Myeongdong – easier with heavy luggage.
Subway tickets, T-money & deposit refund

Three ways to ride: a T-money card (rechargeable, also for buses, taxis and convenience stores), a single-journey card from the station machine, or a visitor/unlimited pass (e.g. Climate Card in Seoul).
T-money: buy at a convenience store (₩3,000–4,000) and top up with CASH at the store or the station top-up machine.
Single-journey card: choose your destination on the ticket machine – the fare includes a ₩500 deposit. After the ride, put the card into the deposit-refund machine (보증금 환급기) to get ₩500 back.
Gates: hold the card flat on the reader until it beeps, then walk through. One card per person – every person taps. Wide gates are for wheelchairs, strollers and big luggage.
Tap OUT at the exit gate too – the fare depends on distance.
Free transfers (환승)
Subway ↔ bus transfers are free or discounted if you transfer within about 30 minutes (longer late at night). The trick: you MUST tap your card when getting OFF the bus too, or you lose the transfer.
Subway lines are numbered AND colour-coded. Follow the colour + station number (e.g. 201).
Use Naver Map or KakaoMap – Google Maps walking/driving directions are limited in Korea.
City buses

Board at the FRONT door and tap, exit at the BACK door and tap again. Press the red STOP button before your stop. Blue = trunk lines, green = local, red = express to suburbs, yellow = downtown loop (Seoul).
Hold on – Korean buses start quickly.
Takeaway drinks without a lid may be refused on Seoul buses.
Taxis & ride apps
Orange/silver/white = regular taxis. BLACK "Deluxe/모범" taxis cost more. Kakao T (main Korean app) and Uber both work in big cities. A late-night surcharge applies around 22:00–04:00. No tipping.
Show the destination in Korean on your phone.
Fasten your seat belt – it is required in back seats too.
KTX high-speed train

Seoul ↔ Busan in about 2.5 h, Seoul ↔ Gyeongju (Singyeongju) about 2 h. Book on the Korail app/website (Korail Talk) – weekends sell out. A KR Pass for foreigners gives unlimited rides for a set number of days.
Be on the platform a few minutes early: trains leave exactly on time.
SRT is a second high-speed line leaving from Suseo (Gangnam).
Bikes & e-scooters
Seoul public bikes (Ttareungyi) can be rented by app. Ride on bike lanes, not crowded sidewalks. Electric kick-scooters legally need a driving licence, a helmet and only ONE rider – fines apply.
Han River parks have long, flat bike paths – perfect at sunset.
Driving: licence & IDP
To rent a car or motorbike you need your home licence, passport and an International Driving Permit (Geneva/Vienna convention) – or a Korean licence. Drive on the RIGHT. Speed cameras are everywhere.
Rental motorbikes require a motorcycle-class licence and a helmet.
Jeju is the most popular self-drive island.
Ferries & ports
International ferries link Busan with Japan (Fukuoka, Osaka, Shimonoseki). Domestic ferries go to Jeju, Ulleungdo and islands. Bring your passport even for domestic ferries – ID is checked.
Ferries can be cancelled in strong wind – keep a buffer day.
Walking & crosswalks
Cross only at crosswalks when the green walker is on – the number shows remaining seconds. Watch for right-turning cars and delivery motorbikes, which may still move. Jaywalking can be fined.
Hotels
Check-in is usually 15:00, check-out 11:00–12:00. Most hotels keep your luggage for free before check-in. Electricity is 220 V with round two-pin plugs (Type C/F).
Airbnb & homestays

Book only listings that show a Korean business registration – unregistered rentals are illegal and can be cancelled. Respect quiet hours in apartments, separate your trash the local way and never use the building's shared spaces for parties.
Motels & guesthouses
Korean motels are cheap, private and usually very clean – walk-in is possible, often with self check-in kiosks. Guesthouses and hostels are the social, budget choice for solo travellers.
Jjimjilbang (Korean spa)

A 24h bathhouse with saunas, a big shared hall and snacks. Entry includes a uniform and towel. The baths are gender-separated and NUDE; wash fully before entering the pool. You can sleep in the common hall cheaply – keep valuables in your locker.
Try sikhye (sweet rice drink) and baked eggs – the classic spa snack.
Roll your towel into the famous "lamb head" (yangmeori) hat.
Hanok stay
Traditional houses with heated floors (ondol). You sleep on a thick mattress (yo) on the floor. Shoes off on the stone step before the wooden floor. Walls are thin – keep voices low at night.
Temple stay
Stay overnight at a Buddhist temple: wake up around 4 am, join chanting, the 108 bows and a silent monastic meal (barugongyang) where you finish every grain. Wear the provided clothes, no alcohol.
Pension (group villa)
Self-catering villas in the countryside or by the sea, popular with families and groups. Many have a BBQ terrace (extra charge for charcoal). Check the max-guest number – extra people cost extra.
Calling the staff

Many tables have a CALL BELL button. Otherwise raise your hand and say "Jeogiyo!" – it is polite, not rude. Water is often self-service, banchan (side dishes) are free and refillable. Pay at the counter on your way out. No tipping.
Bibimbap

Rice topped with vegetables, egg and gochujang (chili paste). MIX everything well with your spoon before eating. In a hot stone bowl (dolsot) leave it a minute so the bottom rice gets crispy (nurungji).
In Korea rice and soup are eaten with a SPOON; chopsticks are for side dishes.
Chimaek (chicken + beer)
Korean fried chicken: crispy "fried", sweet-spicy "yangnyeom" or "ban-ban" (half & half). Pickled radish cubes cleanse the palate. You can even order delivery to a spot in a Han River park.
Baekban (home-style set)

Rice, soup and many side dishes – the everyday Korean meal, cheap and filling. Common at lunch near offices. Some places serve only one menu: just sit down and hold up fingers for the number of people.
Tang & guk (soups)

Seolleongtang & gomtang (beef bone broth) come unsalted – YOU season with salt and green onion on the table. Samgyetang (ginseng chicken) is eaten on the hottest summer days to "fight heat with heat".
Jjigae (stews)
Kimchi-jjigae, doenjang-jjigae (soybean paste), sundubu (soft tofu). Often served in one bubbling pot to share – use your own spoon or a ladle. Very hot: blow and sip!
Dwaeji gukbap (Busan)
Busan's soul food: pork broth with rice. Season it yourself with saeujeot (salted shrimp), chives (buchu) and chili paste. Dip pork slices in saeujeot too.
Korean BBQ: how the table works
Meat (samgyeopsal, moksal, galbi) is grilled on a grill built into your table – staff often grill and cut it for you. Most places need at least 2 portions (2인분 이상).
Smoke pipe: the silver duct above the grill sucks up smoke – pull it down close to the grill.
Scissors & tongs: meat is cut with kitchen scissors, flipped with tongs – there is no knife or fork.
Cutlery drawer: spoons and chopsticks are in a drawer on the side of the table (or a box on it) – set them for everyone.
Storage seats: lift the seat of the stool – put your coat and bag inside so they don't smell of smoke (or ask for a cover/apron).
Finish with "후식 냉면" – a small bowl of cold noodles after the meat – or fried rice in the pan.
Street & market food
Tteokbokki, hotteok (sweet pancake), eomuk (fish cake skewers – the broth is free), gimbap. Hotteok filling is boiling hot sugar: bite carefully. Markets often prefer cash.
Drinking culture

Legal drinking age is 19 (by year). Never pour your own glass – pour for others and they pour for you. Hold the bottle with two hands for elders and turn your head slightly away when drinking in front of them. "Geonbae!" = Cheers.
It is fine to say no: "Jeo-neun an ma-syeo-yo" – I don't drink.
Table manners & meal greetings
Before eating say "잘 먹겠습니다" (I will eat well); when you leave say "잘 먹었습니다" (I ate well) – to your host or to the restaurant staff at the counter.
Don't stick chopsticks upright in rice (it looks like a funeral ritual) and don't lift the rice bowl to your mouth.
Wait for the eldest to start eating; pour drinks for others, not yourself.
Pay at the counter by the exit – no tipping.
Kinds of kimchi
Kimchi comes with almost every meal and refills are free. Making it together in late autumn (gimjang) is UNESCO intangible heritage. Different dishes come with different kimchi:
Baechu-kimchi (napa cabbage, red) – the classic. Baek-kimchi (white kimchi) – no chili, mild and refreshing.
Kkakdugi – cubed radish, crunchy; served with gukbap and seolleongtang. Chonggak-kimchi – whole "ponytail" radishes.
Pa-kimchi – green onion, great with BBQ. Geotjeori – fresh, unfermented "salad" kimchi, often with kalguksu or bossam.
Cut long kimchi with the scissors on the table if needed.
Eating alone & kiosks
Solo dining (honbap) is common now. Many places use kiosks or table tablets with English. Some BBQ/stew places require a 2-person minimum order – look for "1인분 가능" (single portion OK).
Korean banknotes
₩1,000 (blue, Yi Hwang) · ₩5,000 (red-orange, Yi I) · ₩10,000 (green, King Sejong) · ₩50,000 (yellow, Shin Saimdang). ₩5,000 and ₩50,000 look alike in colour – check the number!
Coins
₩10 (gold, Dabotap pagoda), ₩50 (rice plant), ₩100 (Admiral Yi Sun-sin), ₩500 (crane). Coins are used less and less – many cafes are card-only and give no change.
Exchanging money

Airport rates are poor: change only a little there. Licensed money changers in Myeongdong usually give better rates (bring your passport). Unmanned exchange kiosks (e.g. WOWPASS machines) are in hotels and subway stations.
ATMs & banks

Use ATMs marked "Global ATM" / "Foreign Card" (big banks, many convenience stores). Choose ENGLISH on screen and ALWAYS decline "conversion to your currency" (DCC). Banks open about 09:00–16:00 on weekdays.
Cards & mobile pay

Visa/Mastercard work almost everywhere, even for small amounts. Foreign Apple/Google Pay works only at some terminals – carry a physical card. Some apps (Kakao Pay, Naver Pay, Alipay+, WOWPASS) now work with foreign cards or partner wallets.
Exchange rate & budget

Prices are in won (₩, KRW). Drop three zeros for a quick feel: ₩10,000 is roughly 7 USD / 11 AUD (rates move – check a live rate). A simple meal is about ₩10,000–15,000, a coffee ₩4,000–6,000, a subway ride ₩1,500–2,000.
Tax-free shopping
Look for "Tax Free" shops. Show your passport: many stores refund the VAT instantly for qualifying purchases (from about ₩15,000). Otherwise use refund kiosks at the airport before check-in.
Keep right
Walk on the RIGHT on stairs, corridors and sidewalks. On escalators, stand still and hold the handrail. Don't stop suddenly in the middle of a busy flow to take photos.
Queueing
Koreans queue everywhere: subway doors (stand at the side, let people out first), buses, taxi stands, popular restaurants (write your name on the waiting list or use the tablet).
Quiet in public
Subways and buses are quiet: speak softly, no speaker-phone, no loud videos. Avoid eating smelly food on the subway. Residential areas (like Bukchon) are people's homes – whisper.
Priority seats
Seats at the end of subway cars are for the elderly, disabled and pregnant. Pink seats are for pregnant women – leave them empty. Respect for elders is a core value: offer your seat.
Trash & recycling
Public bins are rare – carry a small bag and take trash back to your lodging. Korea separates general waste, recyclables (plastic, cans, paper, glass) and food waste. Empty liquids from cups first.
Shoes off
Take shoes off in homes, hanok, temples' halls, many traditional restaurants with floor seating and jjimjilbang. If you see a step up and shoes lined up – that's your signal.
Two hands & bowing
Give and receive things (money, cards, gifts, drinks) with two hands, or your right hand with the left touching your wrist. A small bow with "Annyeonghaseyo" is the standard greeting.
Photo manners
Ask before photographing people, especially children, elders, haenyeo divers and monks. Shops and pop-ups may ban photos – look for the sign.
Police & tourist police

Emergency: 112. Tourist Police (blue/navy uniform & beret) patrol Myeongdong, Hongdae, Itaewon and other hotspots and speak foreign languages. Lost items: lost112.go.kr or the nearest police box (파출소).
Traffic rules

Drive on the right. Drink-driving limit is 0.03% BAC – just one drink can be too much, and penalties are severe (also for e-scooters & bikes). Right turns on red: stop first and give way to pedestrians. School zones: 30 km/h.
Minor offences (경범죄)
Fines exist for littering, smoking in no-smoking zones (most streets near stations, parks, bus stops), jaywalking, public urination and drunken disorder. Smoke only in marked smoking booths.
Drugs & medicines

Korea has zero tolerance: cannabis is illegal even if legal at home (CBD products too). Some prescription meds (e.g. ADHD stimulants, strong painkillers) are restricted – bring the doctor's note and original packaging, and check before you fly.
Filming, drones & privacy

Secretly filming people is a serious crime. Drones are banned over much of central Seoul and near military sites; you need permission elsewhere. In the DMZ follow the guide: photos are allowed only at marked spots.
Crime prevention

Korea is very safe, but: watch drinks in clubs, use official taxis/apps, beware of "free" street fortune-telling or religious invitations, and keep your passport in the hotel safe (carry a copy). Lost phones are often returned via police.
Bukchon curfew zone

Parts of Bukchon Hanok Village are a "special management zone": tourists may visit only during daytime hours (roughly 10:00–17:00) and fines can apply outside them. People live here – no shouting, no entering gates.
Four seasons

Spring (Mar–May): cherry blossoms, mild, yellow-dust days. Summer (Jun–Aug): hot & humid, monsoon rains (jangma) from late June. Autumn (Sep–Nov): clear skies, red leaves – best season. Winter (Dec–Feb): dry and freezing, often −10 °C in Seoul.
Heatwaves & tropical nights

Recent summers have broken records: 35 °C+ days and nights that stay above 25 °C. Summer now feels longer and autumn heat can last into September–October. Drink water, rest in "heat shelters" (cooling centres) and avoid hiking at midday.
Monsoon, downpours & typhoons

Sudden extreme downpours have become more frequent – underpasses and semi-basement rooms can flood. Typhoons mainly hit Jeju and the south coast in Aug–Sep: flights and ferries get cancelled. Follow the emergency alerts on your phone.
Fine dust (미세먼지)
Some days (mostly late winter–spring) the air quality is bad. Check an AQI app; on "bad" days wear a KF94 mask (sold at convenience stores) and keep outdoor activity short.
Cold waves
Siberian cold snaps bring −15 °C wind chill. Dress in layers, use heat packs (hot packs at convenience stores) and watch for black ice. Warm floors (ondol) make indoors cosy.
Emergency alerts

Your phone may blast loud emergency alerts (heat, rain, earthquake, missing person). They are in Korean (often with English). Install the "Emergency Ready" (Safety Korea) app for alerts and shelters in English.
Cherry-blossom season
Late March–mid April the cherry trees bloom from Jeju and Busan up to Seoul. Festivals (Jinhae, Yeouido, Gyeongju) are packed on weekends, and evenings are still chilly – bring a light jacket.
Go on a weekday morning – weekend festival roads and trains are crowded.
Spring days can also bring yellow dust – check the air quality and carry a mask.
Autumn leaves
Mid October–mid November the mountains turn red and gold, starting in Seoraksan and moving south. It is the busiest hiking season: trails and buses to national parks are crowded at weekends.
Mornings can be near 5 °C and afternoons 20 °C – dress in layers.
The sun sets around 17:30 in November – start hikes early.
Snow & black ice
From December to February snow and "black ice" make pavements and stairs slippery, and mountain roads may need snow chains. Ski resorts in Gangwon open in December.
Wear shoes with grip and hold the handrails on outdoor stairs.
Heat packs (핫팩) from the convenience store keep hands and pockets warm.
Seollal – Lunar New Year

Korea's biggest holiday (late January or February, 3 days). Families travel home, so trains and buses sell out weeks ahead and many small restaurants and markets close. Palaces and museums usually stay open, some with free entry and folk games.
Book KTX and express buses early and check opening days before you go.
Say "새해 복 많이 받으세요" – "Have lots of luck in the new year".
Chuseok – harvest holiday

Korean Thanksgiving (September or early October, 3 days). Roads and trains are packed, many shops and restaurants close for a day or two, and people eat songpyeon rice cakes. Palaces often have free entry and traditional events.
Convenience stores, big chains and tourist areas stay open – plan meals there.
Inter-city travel is hardest on the first and last holiday days.
Pharmacy (약국)

Look for the big "약" sign. Pharmacists can sell many over-the-counter medicines and give advice; some meds need a doctor's prescription. Most close in the evening and on Sundays – search "휴일지킴이 약국" for duty pharmacies.
Medicine at convenience stores

At night, convenience stores sell a limited set of "safe household medicines": painkillers/fever reducers, digestive aids, cold medicine and pain patches. Ask the clerk – they are usually behind the counter.
Che-haet-da – indigestion

Koreans call sudden indigestion after eating too fast "che-haet-da". Pharmacies sell digestive drinks (like the famous herbal ones) and tablets. Rest and warm water help. Severe pain, fever or vomiting → see a doctor.
Clinics & hospitals

For minor illness go to a local clinic (의원/clinic) – walk-in, short wait, affordable even without Korean insurance. Bring your passport. Big university hospitals have International Healthcare Centres with interpreters.
Korean medicine (한의원)

Traditional Korean medicine clinics offer acupuncture, cupping and herbal medicine – a licensed medical profession in Korea. Popular for muscle pain and digestion. Tell the doctor about allergies and current medications.
Emergency room & 119

Call 119 for an ambulance (free, interpreters available) – they also tell you which ER can take you. ERs (응급실) are for real emergencies and cost much more for non-urgent cases. Don't walk in for a cold.
Health insurance

Short-term tourists are NOT covered by Korea's National Health Insurance, so you pay the full (still reasonable) price. Buy travel insurance before you fly and keep all receipts and the medical report (진단서) for your claim.
1330 Travel hotline
Call 1330 (24/7) for free help in English, Japanese, Chinese and more: interpretation with a doctor, taxi driver or police, directions and complaints. From a foreign phone dial +82-2-1330.
First aid basics

Heatstroke: move to shade, cool the body, small sips of water, call 119 if confused. Sprain: rest, ice, compress, elevate. Jellyfish sting: rinse with seawater (not fresh water), remove tentacles with a card. AEDs are in subway stations and big buildings.
Subway: numbers, exits, music & queues
Every line has a number and a colour, and every station a number (e.g. 201 = Line 2, City Hall). Follow the colour and the number on the signs.
Exit numbers: big stations have 10+ exits. Maps and apps tell you which exit (출구) to use – e.g. "Exit 3" – check the yellow exit signs before going up.
Music: in Seoul a short traditional tune plays before a TRANSFER station; announcements are in Korean, English, Chinese and Japanese.
Queues: stand in the marked lines on both sides of the screen door; let people get off first, then board.
Pink seats are for pregnant women; seats at the car ends are for elderly and disabled people.
Convenience stores (편의점)
GS25, CU, emart24 and 7-Eleven are on almost every corner – most open 24 hours. They are more than shops: you can top up T-money, use an ATM, pay bills, pick up parcels and buy basic medicine.
Look for "1+1" and "2+1" stickers – buy one, get one free.
Plastic bags cost a little extra – bring your own or say "봉투 필요 없어요".
Cards and mobile pay work everywhere; T-money can also pay for snacks.
Convenience-store food & how to eat it
Favourites: triangle gimbap, dosirak (lunch boxes), cup ramyeon, banana milk, hot dogs and fried chicken. Many stores have a small eat-in table with a microwave and hot water.
Triangle gimbap: pull tab ① down the middle, then pull corners ② and ③ – the seaweed stays crisp.
Cup ramyeon: open the lid halfway, fill to the inside line with hot water, wait 3–4 minutes.
Dosirak: remove the sauce cup and lid as printed, microwave about 1–2 minutes (check the label).
Using the store machines & eat-in table
Self-service hot-water dispenser, microwave, coffee machine and (in some stores) a self-checkout kiosk. Han River stores even have automatic ramyeon cookers.
Hot water: put the cup under the nozzle and press – mind your fingers.
Ramyeon cooker: buy the paper-bowl ramyeon, put noodles + soup in the bowl, place it on the plate and press start (about 2–3 min).
After eating: pour leftover soup into the sink/food-waste bin, sort cups and cans, wipe the table.
24-hour unmanned stores
Unmanned ice-cream shops, snack stores and late-night convenience stores have no staff – you scan and pay yourself at a kiosk.
Entry: some doors open only after you tap a card or scan a QR code (adult check at night).
Pay: scan each barcode at the kiosk, then pay by card – many take no cash.
Everything is on CCTV – always pay before leaving and keep the receipt.
Ssam & ssamjang: how to wrap
Ssam = a bite wrapped in a leaf. Ssamjang is the thick reddish-brown dip (soybean paste + chili paste) that comes with BBQ.
1) Lettuce or perilla leaf in your palm  2) a piece of meat  3) a dab of ssamjang, garlic, green chili or kimchi  4) fold and eat in ONE bite.
Too big for one bite? Make a smaller one – biting a ssam in half gets messy.
Leaves and side dishes are refilled for free – ask "상추 좀 더 주세요".
Seoul Classic
First-timer's 5 nights / 7 days

Fly in from Australia and survive your first Seoul trip: get out of Incheon Airport, eat and sing in Myeongdong, deal with a sudden "che-haet-da" indigestion, then PLAN two free days yourself – opening days, weather, lunch, energy and the last subway all matter. Your early decisions (insurance, umbrella…) come back later!
Seoul
Incheon International Airport
Stay near Myeongdong or Hongdae: hostels, single-portion restaurants and safe late-night streets.
Book a hanbok set for two at Gyeongbokgung and catch sunset at N Seoul Tower.
Split taxis (max 4 per car), book a big noraebang room and try chimaek by the Han River.
Use airport limousine buses or a van taxi; reserve restaurants for 6+ in advance.
Escape Incheon Airport
Incheon Airport T1
After a 10-hour overnight flight from Sydney you land at Incheon International Airport. Signs are in Korean, English, Chinese and Japanese.
Annyeong! I'm Kachi the magpie – magpies bring good news in Korea. I'll guide your trip!
Quick question before we start – your choices on this trip will come back later. Think ahead!
Back home, before flying: did you buy travel insurance?
Yes – travel insurance for the whole trip (≈₩35,000)
A small cost now… we'll see if it pays off.
No – nothing ever happens to me, I'll save the money
Saved ₩35,000. Let's hope nothing happens…
At immigration the officer asks for your documents. What should you have ready?
Passport + my entry approval (K-ETA/visa if my nationality needs one) + hotel address
Perfect. Rules for K-ETA/visa change – always check the official site before flying.
Just a photo of my passport on my phone
A photo is not accepted. You need the physical passport.
Nothing, Australians never need anything
Visa-waiver rules change from year to year. Check before every trip.
Welcome weather
The arrival screen shows today's weather. Korea has four distinct seasons – and they've been getting more extreme lately.
Airport exchange counter

You need some won for the T-money card and street food. Read the rate board for your currency, decide how much to change at the (expensive) airport counter, count the cash and get to know every Korean note and coin.
You have one big suitcase. Which is the best way into central Seoul?
AREX train to Seoul Station
Fast, cheap and on time. Follow the "Train to Seoul" signs to B1.
Airport limousine bus to Myeongdong
Also great with luggage – it stops near big hotels.
Regular taxi all the way
Possible, but about ₩60,000–90,000 with tolls and a late-night surcharge.
For a group this size, everyone needs their own T-money card – one card can't pay for several people on the subway.
T-money: buy, top up, tap
Buy a T-money card at the convenience store, top it up with cash at the station machine, then get through the ticket gates like a local.
Travelling in January
January is the coldest month: −10 °C mornings, dry air and icy pavements. Seollal (Lunar New Year) can fall in late January.
Travelling in February
February is still freezing, with the last snow. Seollal often falls in February – check holiday closures and book transport early.
Travelling in March
March warms up slowly (0–13 °C). Fine dust and yellow dust are common, and the first blossoms open in the south at the end of the month.
Travelling in April
April is cherry-blossom month – mild days, chilly evenings and crowded festivals. Yellow dust days still happen.
Travelling in May
May is warm and green (15–25 °C) – one of the best months to travel. Children's Day (5 May) and Buddha's Birthday make some days very busy.
Travelling in June
June gets hot and humid, and the monsoon (jangma) usually starts in the last week.
Travelling in July
July is monsoon season: heavy downpours, flooding alerts and steamy 30 °C+ days. Carry an umbrella everywhere.
Travelling in August
August is the hottest month (33 °C+, tropical nights) and typhoons can reach Jeju and the south coast.
Travelling in September
September is still warm, with typhoon risk early in the month. Chuseok often falls in September – expect closures and full trains.
Travelling in October
October has clear blue skies and the first autumn leaves – cool mornings, warm afternoons. Chuseok can fall in early October.
Travelling in November
November brings peak leaves in the south and the first cold snaps in the north. Days are short – plan outdoor visits before 17:00.
Travelling in December
December turns freezing, with the first snow, ski resorts opening and Christmas lights in the cities.
Immigration, baggage claim & customs
Incheon Airport Terminal 1 arrivals
Subway to Myeongdong
Seoul Station → Myeongdong (Line 4)
At Seoul Station you must transfer from AREX to Subway Line 4 (sky-blue) towards Dangogae.
How do you find the right platform?
Follow the light-blue "4" signs and the direction (next station)
Yes! Every line has a colour and a number. Station numbers like 424 help too.
Ask everyone loudly in English
People may help, but the signs are faster – and quieter.
The train arrives. People are lined up at the sides of the doors.
The doors open. What do you do?
Stand aside and let passengers get off first
Correct. Then board quickly and move inside.
Rush in first to get a seat
You blocked people getting off. Just wait beside the doors – let people exit first, then board.
The only empty seats are pink with a pregnant-woman sign, and two at the end of the car for elders. You are tired…
Stay standing and hold the strap
Respect! Pink seats are left empty for pregnant women.
Sit in the pink seat – nobody is pregnant now
Koreans keep this pink seat free for pregnant women, even on busy trains – a kind custom to follow.

Myeongdong check-in & street food
Myeongdong
It's 11:00. Your hotel check-in is at 15:00.
It's 11:00. Your hotel check-in is at 15:00 – and four friends' worth of suitcases is a lot to drag around.
What do you do with your luggage?
Ask the front desk to keep it until check-in
Almost every hotel does this for free.
Drag it around Myeongdong for four hours
Heavy bags on busy streets – tiring! Korea has handy luggage storage and same-day luggage delivery at major stations.
Of course. Here is your tag. Your room will be ready at 3 pm.
You charge your phone – wait, your Australian plug doesn't fit! Korean sockets are 220 V with two round pins. You borrow an adapter from the front desk.
Myeongdong's street food stalls open in the afternoon: tteokbokki, egg bread, grilled cheese lobster, hotteok…
